authors: Luis Garicano, Claire Lelarge, John Van Reenen
title: Firm Size Distortions and the Productivity Distribution: Evidence from France
method: Structural Lucas span-of-control model estimated from bunching of the firm size distribution just below the 50-employee threshold where labour laws bind
finding: The 50-employee rules are equivalent to a 2.3% variable tax on labour; with French real-wage rigidity welfare costs are 3.4% of GDP (1.3% if wages were fully flexible). Workers and large firms lose, small firms gain.
summary_plain: French firms pile up just below 50 employees, where many labour rules start to apply. The authors estimate these rules cost the economy about 3.4% of GDP, mostly at the expense of workers.
relevance: EU digital laws also use size thresholds (e.g. DSA VLOP 45m users, DMA gatekeeper criteria, SME carve-outs), which can create similar bunching and growth disincentives.
caveats: Result depends on the structural model and wage-rigidity assumption; concerns labour law, not digital regulation.

authors: Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud, John Van Reenen
title: The Impact of Regulation on Innovation
method: Endogenous growth model with size-contingent regulation; discontinuity in innovation at the 50-employee threshold plus responses to exogenous export-demand shocks
finding: The share of innovating firms falls sharply just below the 50-employee threshold and their innovation response to demand shocks is muted; regulation reduces aggregate innovation by 5.7% (AER abstract; the 2021 NBER version reported 5.4% and a 2.2% consumption-equivalent welfare loss).
summary_plain: Firms close to a regulatory size threshold innovate less, because growing would bring extra rules. Across France this lowers overall innovation by around 6%.
relevance: Shows that size-based regulatory burdens can depress innovation, the core output EU digital policy aims to protect.
caveats: Effects mainly on incremental innovation; the NBER version finds regulated firms that do innovate pursue more radical breakthroughs.

authors: Simeon Djankov, Rafael La Porta, Florencio Lopez-de-Silanes, Andrei Shleifer
title: The Regulation of Entry
method: New cross-country dataset on procedures, time and official cost to start a business; cross-country correlations
finding: Official entry costs are extremely high in most countries; heavier entry regulation is associated with more corruption and larger unofficial economies but not better public or private goods quality.
summary_plain: Counting the steps, days and fees needed to open a company in 85 countries, the authors find that heavy start-up rules go with more corruption and a bigger informal economy, not better products or services.
relevance: Founding paper of the World Bank Doing Business approach and of counting rules as a measure of regulatory burden, the method this site applies to EU digital law.
caveats: Correlational; measures formal rules on paper, not enforcement or benefits.

authors: Leora Klapper, Luc Laeven, Raghuram Rajan
title: Entry Regulation as a Barrier to Entrepreneurship
geography_period: Western and Eastern Europe, late 1990s (Amadeus firm data)
method: Difference-in-differences across industries: entry in naturally high-entry industries (US benchmark) compared across countries with different entry costs
finding: Costly entry regulations reduce creation of new firms, especially in naturally high-entry industries, force entrants to be larger, and slow growth of incumbents in those industries.
summary_plain: In European countries where starting a company is expensive, fewer new firms appear in sectors that would naturally see many start-ups, and those that do enter start bigger.
relevance: European evidence that fixed regulatory costs filter out small entrants, a key concern for digital markets with many start-ups.
caveats: Cross-sectional identification; US industry entry rates as benchmark may not reflect 'natural' entry everywhere.

title: Does Entry Regulation Hinder Job Creation? Evidence from the French Retail Industry
method: Regional and time variation in zoning-board approvals of large stores, instrumented by the political composition of the boards
finding: Approval requirements created entry barriers that weakened retail employment growth; retail employment could have been more than 10% higher without the regulation.
summary_plain: France required local boards to approve big new shops. Where boards blocked more stores, fewer retail jobs were created; without the rule there might be over 10% more retail jobs.
relevance: Classic evidence that ex-ante approval regimes protecting incumbents cost jobs, relevant to authorisation and gatekeeping-style rules.
caveats: Single sector and country; IV relies on board politics affecting jobs only through approvals.

title: The Cost of Regulatory Compliance in the United States
method: Establishment-level occupation data combined with occupation task content to estimate wage bill spent on compliance; IV to separate requirements from enforcement
finding: Compliance labour costs average 1.34% of a firm's wage bill, rising over time; the share follows an inverted U by size, peaking around 500 employees.
summary_plain: US firms spend on average about 1.3% of their payroll on staff whose work is complying with rules. Mid-sized firms bear the highest share, not the smallest or largest.
relevance: Gives a measured order of magnitude for compliance costs and suggests burdens fall hardest on mid-sized 'scale-ups', where EU digital firms often struggle.
caveats: Counts only labour compliance costs, not capital, external advisers or forgone activity; working paper.

title: Regulatory Intensity and Firm-Specific Exposure
geography_period: United States, listed firms (federal paperwork regulations)
method: Firm-specific regulatory intensity built from administrative paperwork-burden data and machine learning; panel regressions with heterogeneity by financial constraints
finding: Higher regulatory intensity raises costs of goods sold and overhead, and leads firms to cut capital investment, hire fewer employees and lobby more, especially when financially constrained.
summary_plain: Firms facing more federal paperwork rules spend more on overheads, invest and hire less, and lobby more, particularly firms short of cash.
relevance: Firm-level evidence on the channels (cost, uncertainty, lobbying) through which regulatory volume affects investment and jobs.
caveats: Paperwork burden is a partial measure of regulation; listed US firms only.

title: Is Regulation to Blame for the Decline in American Entrepreneurship?
geography_period: United States, industry panel over recent decades (RegData period)
method: Industry panel linking RegData (regulatory restriction counts from the Code of Federal Regulations) to Census measures of startups and job reallocation, with industry and year fixed effects
finding: Rising federal regulation cannot explain the secular decline in startup rates and job reallocation.
summary_plain: US business start-ups and job churn have fallen for decades, but this study finds that the growth in federal rules does not explain that decline.
relevance: Key contrary evidence: counts of regulatory restrictions, like those used on this site, do not necessarily predict lower business dynamism.
caveats: Restriction counts are a crude measure of burden; federal rules only, not state licensing.
interested_party: Uses Mercatus RegData; Tabarrok is a GMU professor affiliated with Mercatus

authors: James B. Bailey, Diana W. Thomas
title: Regulating Away Competition: The Effect of Regulation on Entrepreneurship and Employment
method: Industry fixed-effects regressions of firm births and employment (Statistics of US Businesses) on RegData regulation counts
finding: More-regulated industries had fewer new firm births and slower employment growth; large firms were less likely than small firms to exit heavily regulated industries.
summary_plain: US industries with more federal rules saw fewer new businesses and slower job growth, and big firms coped with the rules better than small ones.
relevance: Supports the concern that rule volume raises entry barriers and favours incumbents, a central argument in debates on digital regulation.
caveats: Fixed-effects correlations; magnitudes not reported in abstract; contrasts with Goldschlag & Tabarrok using similar data.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which builds RegData and advocates regulatory reform

authors: Dustin Chambers, Patrick A. McLaughlin, Tyler Richards
title: Regulation, Entrepreneurship, and Firm Size
method: Industry panel regressions of firm counts and employment by firm size on industry-specific regulatory restrictions
finding: A 10% increase in industry regulatory restrictions is associated with a 0.5% fall in the number of firms of all sizes, but a 0.6% fall in employment only among small firms.
summary_plain: When an industry's rulebook grows, the number of firms falls slightly, and job losses are concentrated in small businesses rather than large ones.
relevance: Quantifies the claim that regulatory growth is regressive by firm size, central to SME-proportionality in EU digital law.
caveats: Associational; small elasticities; restriction counts as burden proxy.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which builds RegData and advocates regulatory reform

authors: Bentley Coffey, Patrick A. McLaughlin, Pietro Peretto
title: The Cumulative Cost of Regulations
method: Multisector Schumpeterian endogenous-growth model whose closed-form solution gives the estimating equation, fitted with RegData 2.2
finding: Regulation has dampened US growth by about 0.8 percentage points per year since 1980; the economy would have been roughly 25% larger in 2012 had regulation stayed at 1980 levels.
summary_plain: By adding up the small yearly drag of accumulating rules, this study estimates the US economy would be about a quarter bigger if federal regulation had stayed at its 1980 level.
relevance: The most-cited estimate of the cumulative macro cost of regulatory accumulation, often invoked in debates about the stock of EU rules.
caveats: Costs only, no benefits measured; large counterfactual extrapolation from model structure.
interested_party: Mercatus Center (George Mason University), which builds RegData and advocates regulatory reform

authors: John W. Dawson, John J. Seater
title: Federal Regulation and Aggregate Economic Growth
method: Time-series measure of federal regulation (pages of the Code of Federal Regulations) in an endogenous growth framework
finding: Regulation has caused substantial reductions in the growth rates of US output and TFP and offers an explanation for the 1970s productivity slowdown (authors' abstract; no single figure verified here).
summary_plain: Using the page count of US federal rules over half a century, the authors conclude that regulation significantly slowed economic and productivity growth.
relevance: Early macro evidence linking the volume of regulatory text to growth, the logic behind counting restrictions in EU law.
caveats: Aggregate time series with few observations; page counts are a coarse proxy; widely debated magnitudes.

title: License to Sell: The Effect of Business Registration Reform on Entrepreneurial Activity in Mexico
method: Difference-in-differences using staggered municipal rollout of a business-registration simplification
finding: Simplifying entry raised registered businesses by 5% and wage employment by 2.2%, while lowering incumbents' income by 3%; informal firms did not register more.
summary_plain: When Mexican towns made it easier to register a business, more people (mainly former employees) opened firms and employment rose, though existing businesses earned somewhat less.
relevance: Quasi-experimental evidence that cutting administrative entry burdens raises entry and jobs, but with modest effects and no formalisation gain.
caveats: Developing-country context; effects modest; only registration procedures, not substantive rules.
interested_party: Author at the World Bank, which promotes business-registration reform

authors: European Commission, DG Enterprise and Industry (Expert Group)
title: Models to Reduce the Disproportionate Regulatory Burden on SMEs: Report of the Expert Group
method: Expert group review of national evidence and good practices on SME regulatory burden
finding: Where a big enterprise spends one euro per employee to comply with a regulatory duty, a medium-sized enterprise might spend around four euros and a small business up to ten euros.
summary_plain: The Commission's experts estimated that, per worker, small firms can pay up to ten times more than large firms to comply with the same rule.
relevance: The source of the EU's 'Think Small First' and SME-test logic, which shapes proportionality and SME exemptions in digital legislation.
caveats: Indicative estimate drawn from earlier studies, not a new causal analysis; dated.
